11.1: These are the properties of the rational soul: it sees itself, analyses itself, and makes itself whatever it chooses; it enjoys the fruit it bears itself—for the fruits of plants, and what corresponds to fruit in animals, others enjoy—and it reaches its own end, wherever the limit of life may be set. It is not as in a dance or a play or such things, where the whole performance is incomplete if anything cuts it short; but in every part, and wherever it may be stopped, it makes what has been set before it full and complete, so that it can say: I have what is my own. And further, it travels through the whole universe and the empty space around it, and surveys its form, and it reaches out into the infinity of time, and embraces and understands the periodic renewal of all things, and it understands that those who come after us will see nothing new, nor have those before us seen anything more; but in a way the man who is forty years old, if he has any understanding at all, has seen, because of the uniformity that prevails, all things that have been and all that will be. This too is a property of the rational soul: love of one's neighbour, and truth and modesty, and valuing nothing more than itself, which is also the property of Law. So right reason does not differ at all from the reason of justice.
11.2: You will set little value on pleasing song and dancing and the pancratium if you break the melody of the voice up into its separate sounds and ask yourself, of each one, whether you are mastered by this; for you will be stopped by shame from admitting it. And in the case of dancing, do the same with each movement and pose; and likewise in the case of the pancratium. In all things, then, except virtue and the acts of virtue, remember to turn to their separate parts, and by this division come to value them little: and apply this rule to your whole life as well.
11.3: What a soul that is which is ready, if at any moment it must be separated from the body, to be either extinguished, or scattered, or to continue to exist! But this readiness must come from a man's own judgement, not from mere obstinacy, as with the Christians, but thoughtfully and with dignity, and in a way that would persuade another, without theatrical display.
11.4: Have I done something for the common good? Well then, I have had my reward. Let this always be present to your mind, and never stop doing such good.
11.5: What is your art? To be good. And how is this done well except by general principles, some about the nature of the universe, and others about the proper constitution of man?
11.6:
At first tragedies were brought on the stage as a means of reminding men of the things that happen to them, and that it is according to nature for things to happen so, and that, if you are delighted with what is shown on the stage, you should not be troubled by what takes place on the larger stage. For you see that these things must be accomplished in this way, and that even those who cry out “O Cithaeron” have to bear them. And indeed, some things are said well by the dramatic writers, such as this one especially:—

“Me and my children if the gods neglect,
This has its reason too.”

And again,—

“We must not chafe and fret at what happens.”

And,—

“Reap life’s harvest like the wheat’s fruitful ear.”

And other things of the same kind.

After tragedy the old comedy was introduced, which had a magisterial freedom of speech, and by its very plain speaking was useful in reminding men to beware of insolence; and for this purpose Diogenes too used to borrow from these writers.

But as to the middle comedy, which came next, observe what it was, and again, for what purpose the new comedy was introduced, which gradually sank into a mere imitative artifice. That some good things are said even by these writers, everybody knows: but the whole design of such poetry and drama, what end does it look to?
11.7: How plain it is that there is no other condition of life so well suited for philosophising as the one you now happen to be in.
11.8: A branch cut off from the branch next to it must necessarily be cut off from the whole tree too. So too a man, when he is separated from another man, has fallen away from the whole social community. Now a branch is cut off by someone else; but a man separates himself from his neighbour by his own act when he hates him and turns away from him, and he does not know that he has at the same time cut himself off from the whole social system. Yet he certainly has this privilege from Zeus, who framed society: it is in our power to grow back on to what is next to us, and again to become a part that helps to make up the whole. However, if this kind of separation happens often, it makes it difficult for what detaches itself to be brought back to unity and restored to its former condition. Finally, the branch which grew together with the tree from the first, and has continued to share one life with it, is not like one that is grafted on after being cut off; for this is something like what the gardeners mean when they say that it grows with the rest of the tree, but does not share the same mind with it.
11.9: Just as those who try to stand in your way when you are going forward according to right reason will not be able to turn you aside from your proper action, so do not let them drive you from your kindly feelings towards them either; but be on your guard equally in both matters, not only in steady judgement and action, but also in gentleness towards those who try to stop or otherwise trouble you. For this too is a weakness, to be irritated with them, just as it is to be turned from your course of action and to give way through fear; for both are equally deserters from their post—the man who does it through fear, and the man who is estranged from one who is by nature his kinsman and friend.
11.10: There is no nature which is inferior to the arts, for the arts imitate the natures of things. But if this is so, the nature which is the most perfect and the most comprehensive of all natures cannot fall short of the skill of art. Now all arts do the lower things for the sake of the higher; so the universal nature does too. And indeed, this is the origin of justice, and in justice the other virtues have their foundation: for justice will not be kept if we either care for things that are indifferent, or are easily deceived and careless and changeable.
11.11: If the things whose pursuit and avoidance disturb you do not come to you, still in a way you go to them. Let your judgement about them be at rest, then, and they will stay quiet, and you will not be seen either pursuing or avoiding them.
11.12: The soul keeps its spherical form when it is neither stretched out towards any object, nor drawn in on itself, nor scattered, nor sinking down, but is lit by a light by which it sees the truth—the truth of all things and the truth that is in itself.
11.13: Suppose someone despises me. Let him see to that himself. But I will see to this: that I am not found doing or saying anything that deserves contempt. Will someone hate me? Let him see to it. But I will be gentle and kindly towards every man, and ready to show even him his mistake, not reproachfully, nor as if making a display of my patience, but nobly and honestly, like the great Phocion, unless indeed he was only pretending. For the inner parts ought to be like this, and a man ought to be seen by the gods neither dissatisfied with anything nor complaining. For what evil is it to you, if you are now doing what is in keeping with your own nature, and are satisfied with what at this moment suits the nature of the universe, since you are a human being placed at your post so that what is for the common good may be done in some way?
11.14: Men despise one another and flatter one another; and men wish to raise themselves above one another, and grovel before one another.
11.15: How unsound and insincere is the man who says, I have decided to deal with you fairly!—What are you doing, man? There is no need to give this notice. It will soon show itself in actions. The voice ought to be plainly written on the forehead. Whatever a man's character is, he shows it at once in his eyes, just as the one who is loved at once reads everything in the eyes of his lovers. The man who is honest and good ought to be exactly like a man who smells strong, so that anyone standing by, as soon as he comes near him, must smell it whether he wants to or not. But a pretence of simplicity is like a crooked stick. Nothing is more disgraceful than a wolf's friendship, a false friendship. Avoid this above all. The good and simple and kindly show all these things in their eyes, and there is no mistaking it.
11.16: As to living in the best way, this power is in the soul, if it is indifferent to things that are indifferent. And it will be indifferent if it looks at each of these things both separately and as a whole, and if it remembers that not one of them produces in us an opinion about itself, nor comes to us; but these things stay still, and it is we ourselves who produce the judgements about them and, as we might say, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, if by chance these judgements have slipped unnoticed into our minds, to wipe them out; and if it remembers too that such attention will only be needed for a short time, and then life will be over. Besides, what trouble is there at all in doing this? For if these things are according to nature, rejoice in them and they will be easy for you: but if they are contrary to nature, look for what is in keeping with your own nature, and strive towards this, even if it brings no reputation; for every man is allowed to seek his own good.
11.17: Consider where each thing has come from, and what it consists of, and what it changes into, and what kind of thing it will be when it has changed, and that it will suffer no harm.
11.18:
If anyone has offended against you, consider first: what my relation to men is, and that we are made for one another; and in another respect I was made to be set over them, as a ram over the flock or a bull over the herd. But examine the matter from first principles, from this: if all things are not mere atoms, it is nature that orders all things; if this is so, the lower things exist for the sake of the higher, and these for the sake of one another.

Second, consider what kind of men they are at table, in bed, and so on; and especially, what compulsions their opinions put them under; and as to their acts, consider with what pride they do what they do.

Third, that if men are right to do what they do, we ought not to be displeased: but if they are not right, it is plain that they act involuntarily and in ignorance. For just as every soul is unwillingly deprived of the truth, so too is it unwillingly deprived of the power of behaving towards each man as he deserves. That is why men are pained when they are called unjust, ungrateful, and greedy, and in a word wrongdoers to their neighbours.

Fourth, consider that you too do many things wrong, and that you are a man like others; and even if you do refrain from certain faults, you still have the disposition to commit them, even though it is through cowardice, or concern for reputation, or some such mean motive, that you refrain from them.

Fifth, consider that you do not even understand whether men are doing wrong or not, for many things are done with a view to circumstances. And in short, a man must learn a great deal before he can pass a correct judgement on another man's acts.

Sixth, consider, when you are very irritated or grieved, that man's life is only a moment, and after a short time we are all laid out dead.

Seventh, that it is not men's acts which disturb us, for those acts have their foundation in men's ruling principles, but it is our own opinions which disturb us. Take away these opinions, then, and resolve to let go of your judgement about an act as if it were something terrible, and your anger is gone. How then shall I take away these opinions? By reflecting that no wrongful act of another brings shame on you: for unless what is shameful is the only bad thing, you too must necessarily do many things wrong, and become a robber and everything else.

Eighth, consider how much more pain is brought on us by the anger and irritation caused by such acts than by the acts themselves, at which we are angry and irritated.

Ninth, consider that a good disposition is invincible if it is genuine, and not a put-on smile and the playing of a part. For what will the most violent man do to you, if you continue to be kindly disposed towards him, and if, as the opportunity arises, you gently advise him and calmly correct his errors at the very time when he is trying to do you harm, saying: Not so, my child: we are made by nature for something else: I shall certainly not be harmed, but you are harming yourself, my child.—And show him with gentle tact and by general principles that this is so, and that even bees do not do as he does, nor any animals which are made by nature to live in herds. And you must do this neither with any double meaning nor by way of reproach, but affectionately and without any bitterness in your soul; and not as if you were lecturing him, nor so that some bystander may admire you, but either when he is alone, and if others are present...

Remember these nine rules, as if you had received them as a gift from the Muses, and begin at last to be a man while you live. But you must equally avoid flattering men and being irritated with them, for both are unsociable and lead to harm. And in the excitement of anger let this truth be present to you: that to be moved by passion is not manly, but that mildness and gentleness, as they are more in keeping with human nature, so too are they more manly; and the one who has these qualities has strength, nerve, and courage, not the man who is subject to fits of passion and discontent. For the nearer a man's mind is to freedom from all passion, the nearer it is also to strength: and just as the sense of pain is a mark of weakness, so too is anger. For the one who gives in to pain and the one who gives in to anger are both wounded and both submit.

But if you will, receive also a tenth present from Apollo, the leader of the Muses, and it is this: that to expect bad men not to do wrong is madness, for whoever expects this wants the impossible. But to allow men to behave like this to others, and to expect them not to do you any wrong, is unreasonable and tyrannical.
11.19: There are four chief ways in which the ruling faculty goes astray, which you should constantly be on your guard against, and when you have detected them, you should wipe them out and say on each occasion: This thought is not necessary: this tends to destroy social union: this which you are about to say does not come from your real thoughts; for you should consider it among the most absurd of things for a man not to speak from his real thoughts. But the fourth is when you reproach yourself for anything, for this is evidence that the more divine part within you is being overpowered and is yielding to the less honourable and perishable part, the body, and to its gross pleasures.
11.20: Your airy part and all the fiery parts mingled in you, though by nature they tend upwards, are still, in obedience to the order of the universe, held down here in the compound mass of the body. And also the whole of the earthy part in you and the watery, though they tend downwards, are still raised up and occupy a position which is not their natural one. In this way, then, the elemental parts obey the universal; for when they have been fixed in any place, they must remain there until the universal once more sounds the signal for dissolution. Is it not strange, then, that your intelligent part alone should be disobedient and discontented with its own place? And yet no force is imposed on it, but only those things which are in keeping with its nature: still it does not submit, but is carried in the opposite direction. For the movement towards injustice and intemperance, and to anger and grief and fear, is nothing other than the act of one who strays from nature. And also when the ruling faculty is discontented with anything that happens, then too it deserts its post: for it is made for piety and reverence towards the gods no less than for justice. For these qualities too are included under the general term of contentment with the order of things, and indeed they come before acts of justice.
11.21: He who does not have one and always the same aim in life cannot be one and the same all through his life. But what I have said is not enough, unless this is added too: what this aim ought to be. For just as there is not the same opinion about all the things which the majority consider good in one way or another, but only about certain things, that is, things which concern the common interest, so too we ought to set before ourselves an aim which is social and political. For he who directs all his own efforts to this aim will make all his acts alike, and so will always be the same.
11.22: Think of the country mouse and the town mouse, and of the alarm and panic of the town mouse.
11.23: Socrates used to call the opinions of the many by the name of Lamiae—bogeymen to frighten children.
11.24: The Lacedaemonians, at their public spectacles, used to set seats in the shade for strangers, but themselves sat down anywhere.
11.25: Socrates excused himself to Perdiccas for not going to him, saying: It is because I do not want to perish by the worst of all ends; that is, I do not want to receive a favour and then be unable to return it.
11.26: In the writings of the Ephesians there was this rule: to think constantly of one of the men of former times who practised virtue.
11.27: The Pythagoreans tell us to look to the heavens in the morning, so that we may be reminded of those bodies which always do the same things and do their work in the same way, and also be reminded of their purity and nakedness. For there is no veil over a star.
11.28: Consider what kind of man Socrates was when he dressed himself in a skin, after Xanthippe had taken his cloak and gone out, and what Socrates said to his friends who were ashamed of him and drew back from him when they saw him dressed like that.
11.29: Neither in writing nor in reading will you be able to lay down rules for others before you have first learned to obey rules yourself. This is much more so in life.
11.30: You are a slave: free speech is not for you.
11.31:
And my heart laughed within me.
Homer, Odyssey, ix. 413.
11.32:
And they will curse virtue, speaking harsh words.
Hesiod, Works and Days, 184.
11.33: To look for a fig in winter is a madman's act: such is the man who looks for his child when it is no longer allowed.
11.34: When a man kisses his child, said Epictetus, he should whisper to himself, “Tomorrow perhaps you will die.”—But those are words of bad omen.—“No word is a word of bad omen,” said Epictetus, “which expresses any work of nature; or if it is, then it is also a word of bad omen to speak of the ears of corn being reaped”.
11.35: The unripe grape, the ripe bunch, the dried grape: all are changes, not into nothing, but into something which does not yet exist.
11.36: No one can rob us of our free will.
11.37: Epictetus also said that a man must find an art, or rules, for giving his assent; and as to his impulses, he must take care that they are made with regard to circumstances, that they are consistent with the common good, and that they have regard to the value of the object; and as for sensual desire, he should keep away from it altogether; and as for aversion, he should not show it towards any of the things which are not in our power.
11.38: So the dispute, he said, is not about any ordinary matter, but about being mad or not.
11.39: Socrates used to say: What do you want, the souls of rational men or irrational?—The souls of rational men.—Of what rational men, sound or unsound?—Sound.—Why then do you not seek them?—Because we have them.—Why then do you fight and quarrel?
